earlier_scan.note: No grammar/phonology in Glottolog refs; only lexical-classification work (Hull 1998, Mandala 1999) and oral-literature archive.

sources.citation: Hull, Geoffrey. 2000. Historical Phonology of Tetum. Studies in Languages and Cultures of East Timor 3: 158-212. Academy of East Timor Studies, University of Western Sydney / Instituto Nacional de Linguistica. (archive.org item studies-in-languages-and-cultures-of-east-timor-inl-vol-3; whole-volume scanned text downloaded.)
sources.note: Nothing about Kairui-Midiki (Kawaimina) prosody. The article is a historical phonology of Tetum: it says Proto-Timoric inherited 'a vowel system of five phonemes which could be tonic or atonic' and conditions Tetum sound changes on tonic / pretonic / post-tonic position, but every mention of Kawaimina, Midiki, Kairui, Waimaha or Naueti is a segmental correspondence ([w] < *b in 'North Atauran, Kawaimina and Habu'; initial *z 'survives phonemically in Kawaimina dialects, cf. Waimaha dasu, Naueti yasu, Midiki ijasu, Kairui yoso'; rhotic outcome of *l; retention of *y, *h). A a full-text search…

sources.citation: Glottolog 5.x languoid page and full reference table for kair1265 (5 refs: Hull 1998; Mandala 1999; Moseley 2010; Ethnologue 16; World Oral Literature Project; 0 grammar/phonology/sketch)
sources.note: Bibliographic only; confirms no descriptive work is registered for the language.

sources.citation: English Wikipedia, 'Kairui-Midiki language' (wikitext downloaded 2026-09-17)
sources.note: Stub: classification, speaker numbers, geography (refs Ethnologue, Hull 2004). No phonology, nothing on stress. German Wikipedia 'Midiki' and 'Kawaimina' also checked online (read-online): demographic/geographic only, no Betonung/Akzent content.

sources.citation: Grimes, Charles E. & Owen Edwards. 2026. The Austronesian languages of eastern Indonesia and Timor-Leste: Unravelling their prehistory and classification (Languages of the New Guinea Region 1). Berlin: Language Science Press. 948 pp.
sources.note: sound-change evidence only (Midiki *schwa > i,a; *-ay/*-aw > a shared with Waima'a, Naueti; *uy > i; *ng > n); no stress or tone statement.

sources.citation: Kline, Andrew L. 2026. klinemidiki v1.0.1: Kairui-Midiki fieldwork wordlist (CLDF Wordlist, 1,376 forms / 1,181 concepts, Midiki as spoken in Venilale, Baucau; includes raw FLEx LIFT export of the 'Kairui-Midiki fieldwork dictionary', Kaipuleohone collection ALK1). Zenodo. DOI 10.5281/zenodo.22667173 (concept DOI 10.5281/zenodo.22667172). CC-BY-4.0.
sources.note: No prosodic statement and no stress marks in any of the 1,406 LIFT lexemes (0 occurrences of a stress mark; 2 <pronunciation> fields, both segmental variants). Phonological content is segmental only: orthography profile etc/ defines aspirated kh th, voiceless sonorants mh nh wh lh, a glottalized series k' t' p' m' n' r' l' s' w', intervocalic glottal stop, loan-only ng j x; three notes typed 'phonology' record free variation (maa~mai, weli~yeli, wii~yii) and a general note 'Words ending in ae seem to be in free variance with aa in some speakers'. Wordlist/dictionary data, not a description.

sources.citation: Kline, Andrew. 2026. Documenting the languages of Timor-Leste in the face of Tetun Dili: a case study from the Kairui-Midiki language. Abstract in: I Simposio AIASEAS 'Timor-Leste e o Sudeste Asiatico como Campos de Reflexao', Livro de Resumos / Book of Abstracts, Madrid, 4, p. 48 (Panel 9).
sources.note: No phonology content. Documentation-status statement (verbatim): 'Recent bibliographic work (Ross 2025) confirms that this gap is acute for the Kawaimina language group, where Kairui-Midiki lacks any grammar, dictionary, or substantial primary corpus. This paper presents findings from ten weeks of community-based fieldwork in Venilale Administrative Post, Baucau Municipality documenting Midiki as spoken there. This is the first documentation effort for this variety.' The talk (recorded naturalistic/elicited speech, narrative texts) is the likeliest future source of a prosodic description.

sources.citation: Culhane, Kirsten. 2024. The prosodic foot: A typological study of greater Timor languages. Inaugural-Dissertation (Dr. phil.), Philologische Fakultaet, Albert-Ludwigs-Universitaet Freiburg i. Br. (defended 19.01.2024). DOI 10.6094/UNIFR/243922.
sources.note: phonotactics only (5 vowels, vowel sequences ia iu eo ai au oi oe oa ou ui, codas /k n/, consonant clusters); stress is explicitly NOT used as evidence anywhere in the thesis ('for these languages, there is a lack of empirical evidence for stress', fn.3 p.165, a generic remark that 'the penultimate syllable is described as stressed in GTLs' naming no target language); Midiki listed among languages 'for which there is very little data available' (p.195). No stress statement for Midiki.

sources.citation: Klamer, Marian & Francesca R. Moro (eds.). 2023. Traces of Contact in the Lexicon: Austronesian and Papuan Studies. Leiden/Boston: Brill. DOI 10.1163/9789004529458. (incl. ch. 6: Schapper, Antoinette & Juliette Huber, 'Entwined Histories: The Lexicons of Kawaimina and Maka Languages', 180-209; ch. 8: Gerstner-Link, Claudia, 'Multilateral Lexical Transfer among Four Papuan Language Families: Border, Nimboran, Sentani, and Sko', 263-306; ch. 3 Klamer on Timor-Alor-Pantar/Austronesian contact, 57-100; ch. 5 Fricke on Lamaholot, 140-179; ch. 7 Moro, Sulistyono & Kaiping on Alorese, 213-262.)
sources.note: Nothing. Ch. 6 introduces the group ('four closely related languages: Waima'a, Naueti, Kairui and Midiki, known collectively since Hull (1998) as "Kawaimina" languages', p180; 'Midiki and Kairui (iso 639-3 code: krd), the latter with less than 4,000 speakers, are the smallest of these languages', p182) and then compares lexicons/loan strata with Makasae-Makalero-Fataluku; the only phonological remarks concern loan adaptation (echo-vowel paragoge, p~190). 0 occurrences of stress/tone/accent/prosod- in the chapter.

sources.citation: Schapper, Antoinette & Juliette Huber. 2023. Entwined histories: the lexicons of Kawaimina and Maka languages. In Marian Klamer & Francesca Moro (eds.), Traces of Contact in the Lexicon: Austronesian and Papuan Studies, 180-209. Leiden: Brill. DOI 10.1163/9789004529458_007 (OA, OAPEN)
sources.note: Nothing on stress for Kairui/Midiki. p.184 states the documentation situation: 'Kairui and Midiki are both poorly documented. We only had access to the word lists of Dawson (2014) available in the paradisec archive, and the comparative Kawaimina Swadesh list provided in Veloso (2016).' Only stress-adjacent passage (p.198) concerns Makasae echo vowels.

sources.note: notes only that the Kawaimina dialects are linguistically distinct from one another and geographically discontinuous (citing Hull 2001a: 5); nothing on sound system or prosody.

sources.note: About the SISTER language Waima'a (waim1252), not Kairui-Midiki: conclusion (sec. 7) 'It has no lexical tone. It has no lexical accent and hence also no intonational pitch accent. Intonation units are primarily characterised by a phrase accent on the penultimate syllable and a phrase-final boundary tone.' Does not mention Kairui or Midiki.

sources.citation: Chan, Eugene S. L. (comp.). 2006 [data dated 17 June 1996]. Numeral Systems of the World's Languages: Kairui-Midiki. Leipzig: MPI-EVA lingweb. Data (numerals 1-2000, 'based on Midiki dialect') supplied by Dr. Geoffrey Hull, Instituto Nacional de Linguistica, East Timor.
sources.note: Wordlist-only data: c. 40 numeral forms in broad IPA with vowel length (seː, boseː, kineː, kihɔː) and ɾ, zero stress marks (no ˈ ˌ or accents) and no remark on stress, accent or tone; the only comment is typological (decimal system, Papuan-derived vocabulary, Austronesian structure) and demographic. Not a description; no statement.

sources.citation: Hull, Geoffrey / Instituto Nacional de Linguística. 2004. The Languages of East Timor: Some Basic Facts. Dili: INL, UNTL.
sources.note: Kawaimina section ( lines 192-228): dialect geography of Kairui, Waimaha, Midiki, Naueti; 'remarkable archaisms and strange innovations (e.g. vowel harmony, aspirated and postglottalized consonants)'; numerals 1-10 for Kairui and Midiki. Zero hits for stress/accent in the whole booklet — silent.

sources.citation: Hajek, John & John Bowden. 2002. A phonological oddity in the Austronesian area: Ejectives in Waimoa. Oceanic Linguistics 41(1): 222-224.
sources.note: Mentions Kairui-Midiki only as Waimoa's closest relative/neighbour, reportedly mutually intelligible, and lacking the Waimoa ejectives; nothing on stress.

sources.note: Hull's founding Kawaimina paper with Kairui and Midiki wordlists; may contain transcription conventions or brief phonological notes (incl. accent) for each variety. WSU ResearchDirect unreachable on 2026-09-16 and -17.

sources.citation: Hull, Geoffrey. 1998. The languages of Timor 1772-1997: a literature review. Studies in Languages and Cultures of East Timor 1: 1-38. [same archive.org volume as work 2]
sources.note: No phonology of Kairui/Midiki. Useful pointers only: early-20th-century 'catechisms, prayer-books and Gospel translations were also prepared by various priests in the Tetum, Galoli, Makasai, Midiki and Mambai vernaculars' (p.21); Fr Manuel Neto's lost 'Dicionario da lingua uaima'a'; correction of Fox/Wurm's claim that Kairui and Midiki vocabulary is 'predominantly Papuan'; Capell 1944 misclassified Kairui.

sources.note: Nothing: 'Kairui is entirely a mountain language of small extent. It was not recorded, but its classification is accepted on the word of other natives.' The stress remarks elsewhere in the article concern Capell's transcription of other languages (e.g. Bunak, Makasai), not Kairui.
